lines: Last time, a value was written and then a flag was flipped to announce it, both with the weakest ordering available — and a reader was caught seeing the flag before the value it was supposed to announce.
Two words close that gap for good, and this is where they earn their keep.
Keep the value's own write exactly as weak as before, but change only the flag: the write side now carries a stronger promise, and the matching read side asks for that same stronger promise back.
Does that one change, on just the flag, actually close the gap the earlier run exposed?
answer: Yes, and nothing else about the program had to change at all.
A matched pair like this hands off a guarantee directly from the writer to the reader, which is exactly the piece that was missing before.

lines: The same exhaustive search that found the earlier violation was pointed at this fixed version, exploring every ordering the language actually allows.
Not one of them lets the reader see the flag before the value arrives.
Here's why the pairing actually works: the stronger write carries every earlier write on that same thread along with it, handed to whichever read later asks for the matching stronger guarantee.
That read, once it receives the handoff, then carries its own promise forward — everything it does afterward is guaranteed to come after what it just received.
steps.takeaway: The stronger write carries every earlier write on that thread before the matching stronger read; that read then carries everything after it comes after that handoff.

lines: Suppose only the writing side gets the stronger treatment, and the reading side is left exactly as weak as it started.
The exhaustive search finds the identical bad case all over again — seeing the flag set while the value underneath is still stale.
steps.takeaway: Both sides of the pair have to ask for the stronger guarantee; a stronger write alone promises nothing to a reader that never asked for it.

lines: Now picture two threads with no single leader between them: each one writes its own flag, then checks the other thread's flag, both ends using that same matched stronger pairing from before.
Does the pairing that fixed everything so far still rule out both threads seeing the other's flag as unset?
answer: No — this particular shape slips right through that pairing.
The pairing only ever promised a handoff between the one writer and the one reader directly involved; it never promised a single shared order that every thread in the picture agrees on.

lines: The exhaustive search was pointed at exactly that two-sided shape, every access carrying the matched stronger pairing on both ends.
It still finds a path where both threads see the other's flag as unset, at the exact same moment.
steps.takeaway: The matched pairing only orders the one handoff that actually happens; it gives no single order that every thread involved agrees on at once.

lines: The strongest ordering the language offers adds exactly one more thing on top of everything already covered: every thread, without exception, agrees on one single order for every operation marked this way.
That single shared order is the one thing missing from the two-sided case, and it's the only reason this strongest ordering exists at all.
steps.takeaway: The strongest ordering keeps every earlier guarantee and adds a single order every thread agrees on, which is exactly what the two-sided shape needed.

lines: A standalone checkpoint can do the same handoff work without being tied to any one specific read or write: a lock's own compare-and-swap loop stays as weak as possible, and a separate checkpoint right after winning the lock does the strong-read half of the handoff on its own.
The strong-write half, releasing the lock, still happens the usual way.
steps.takeaway: A standalone checkpoint pairs with a matching operation or another checkpoint the same way the matched pairing does; it just isn't tied to one specific access.

lines: Not every atomic operation needs any of this at all: several independent counters, each one touched by its own set of threads, with nothing ever handed from one thread to another through them.
The weakest ordering was never a shortcut here — it was always the entire, correct story, because there's nothing being published for a stronger guarantee to protect.
steps.takeaway: The weakest ordering is the correct choice, not a shortcut, whenever nothing is actually being handed off from one thread to another.

lines: The matched pairing, proven both ways now, closes a handoff cleanly; the strongest ordering exists for the one narrow shape where a shared, single order across every thread is the actual requirement, not a safety margin someone reached for out of caution.
Every guarantee covered across this chapter has been about memory that's already running becoming visible to another thread that's already running too.
What comes next asks something stranger: what does it mean for a piece of work to not be running yet at all, waiting for something else entirely to decide when it starts.
